en: The *Prakaraṇapañcikā*, composed by the Great Professor Śālikanātha Miśra, who bore the burden of the tradition of the illustrious Guru Prabhākara.
Adorned with the commentary titled *Nyāyasiddhi* and with critical notes (*ṭippaṇī*) on difficult passages,
[this work] is now entitled *Viṣayakaraṇīya*.
The Twelfth Chapter:
Declaration of the Chapter’s Subject Matter.
Having thoroughly examined the system of Prabhākara, this [work] is composed by me.
The description of reasoning is for the purpose of distinguishing both the object and the instrument. // 1 //

In injunctions such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," the person desiring heaven, being connected as the one to be impelled (niyojya), is not capable of relating to an action that is not a means to heaven by way of being its cognizer.

Since action (*kriyā*) is momentary, it is not capable of being the means for attaining heaven and the like, which occur at a later time; therefore, it is established that the optative suffixes (*liṅ* etc. signify an *apūrva*—an effect distinct from the action—that persists until the later time. This concludes the description of our own system.
And the "effect" (kārya) is said to be that which is desired by the agent (kṛti).

"Agentive effort" (kṛti), "the operation of the self" (ātmavyāpāra), and "human exertion" (puruṣaprayatna) are synonymous. Furthermore, the conscious self enters into the effect through its role as the cognizer.
Furthermore, one thing cannot be perceived as an effect belonging to another by virtue of being produced through the operation of that other;
therefore, the effort (prayatna), which is the self's own operation and is to be apprehended through mental perception (mānasapratyakṣa), is what produces it.
Consequently, the self regards the apūrva as the very effect brought about by that [effort].

Since it must indeed be an effort (*prayatna*), that which is the operation of the self— the agent who brings [the result] about— acting as the instigator with respect to the *apūrva*, is expressed by the term "bhāvanā" (productive activity). Furthermore, it is not possible for the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others to denote an effect (*kārya*) without denoting an effort (*kṛti*).
They assert that [the word] denotes both the action (kṛti) and the unseen potency (apūrva);
nor is there any fault in denoting multiple things simultaneously, since such is the way they are understood.
And because of consistency:
for it has been understood through a means of valid cognition that the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth denote an action to be accomplished (*kārya*),
because of that consistency.
The action (*kṛti*), being subordinate, resides in the primary locus—the effect whose nature is *apūrva*.
Furthermore, there is no dispute that even for verbal suffixes such as the optative (*liṅ*) which denote the effect, the number residing in the agent and so forth is expressed.
Nor does the fact of being merely denoted establish that the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) alone is the meaning of the sentence.

Since that which is to be brought about— the *apūrva*— is denoted as a subordinate element (*guṇabhāvena*), while the *apūrva* itself is denoted as the primary element (*pradhānabhāvena*), it follows that this alone constitutes the meaning of the sentence; thus, there is nothing inconsistent.
For this very reason, the venerable Bhāṣyakāra employs the following terminology in various places: "The human effort—the instrument—is called *bhāvanā* with respect to the *apūrva*.
This introduces the fact that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the object (*viṣaya*). That such an effect must necessarily be delimited by some meaning of a verbal root (*bhāvārtha*).
For there is no effort without an objective entity (*bhāvārtha*).
Indeed, every human effort necessarily relies upon some objective entity, because without that [entity], such effort cannot exist.
Therefore, the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), which is invariably concomitant with effort, delimits the *apūrva* as that which is to be accomplished by effort.

Its status as an object (*viṣayabhāva*) consists precisely in its being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatā*). For when something exists in a particular instance and not elsewhere, [it serves as its delimitation].
"He is the object of that" is the view of those who know the object (*viṣayavid*).
And it is said: "The meaning of the word 'object' (*viṣaya*) is existence (*bhāva*) not elsewhere.
Therefore, the object is indeed that which is to be brought into being (*bhāvya*).
Because that which is to be brought into being (bhāvya) alone is the object of human effort,

the word denoting the action (bhāvārtha), as a term for the ritual act (karmaśabda), first deserves to be mentioned in syntactic coordination with words expressing the result (kārya), solely by virtue of its capacity to make known the objective (viṣaya); for it is the necessary adjunct to the comprehension [of the result].
For an unprecedented effect (*apūrva*), being beyond the scope of perception, cannot be understood;
and once an effect is understood, there arises a requirement for its means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).
Therefore, the connection of verbal roots (*bhāvārtha*) with the unprecedented effect is not through their status as subordinate means.

However, considering only the means of comprehension (*pratītyupāyatā*), the Blessed One says: "For the knowledge of an injunction does not arise from an injunction that lacks an object" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka-ṭīkā*).
This is the determination of the verbal root's meaning as the instrument (*karaṇa*).

And that purpose of the injunction (*vidhyartha*), which consists of the task (*kārya*) and is delimited by the verbal action (*bhāvārtha*) that has become its object, is understood as the instrument once it is perceived.
And it requires the manner of performance (*itikartavyatā*),
because that is observed even in other cases where something is to be accomplished;
in that context, it is determined that the very same objective entity (*bhāvārtha*), having become the object, is the instrument (*karaṇa*).
Because it is pervaded by the action (*kṛti*).
For that which is made the object by an action directed toward another purpose is itself the instrument (*karaṇa*) therein.

Just as an axe, being pervaded by the upward-lifting and downward-striking motions which are directed toward the effect characterized by the splitting of wood, is designated as the "instrument" (karaṇa) of those two very motions— which are expressed by the verbal root *chid* and are termed "splitting" because they are delimited by the result characterized by the act of becoming two—

so too here, the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*), being pervaded by the human effort directed toward a new purpose (*apūrva*), is the instrument within that very effort which consists of the production of the unseen potency (*apūrvabhāvanā*).
Now, how can that which has acquired its own nature through effort—the meaning of the verbal root—be the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the productive operation (*bhāvanā*)?
For, by virtue of being the object to be produced (*bhāvyamānatā*), it would indeed be the object (*karman*).
To this, it is said:
In that context, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is not the object (*karman*), because it is the objective of the effort (*kṛti*) directed toward the *apūrva*.
For all factors of action (*kāraka*), with the exception of the agent (*kartṛ*), are pervaded by the activity of that agent.
Yet, they do not thereby attain the status of objects (*karman*),
because they are not intended (*anīpsita*).
Indeed, the status of being an object is observed even in certain cases where something is unintended.
For example: "He performs the Agnihotra sacrifice" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.5.9).

Although an instrument is not possible for the sake of the cessation of its own nature, nevertheless, since the form of the production of the unprecedented (apūrva-bhāvanā) depends upon it, this is not untenable.
Just as in the case of an axe; for the axe is not the object (karman), but rather it is the instrument (karaṇa).
Because it is not intended as the primary object;

for when the raising and lowering [of the axe] are influenced by their connection with the axe, they assume the status of being causes for the act of splitting, since they bring about the result of becoming two-fold.
Therefore, the use of the instrumental case in the injunction “one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*” (*udbhidā yajeta*) is justified.
Because the sacrifice functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the production of the unprecedented potency (*apūrva*), and because the word *udbhid* is its name;
thus, there is only a single productive operation (*bhāvanā*) for both the unprecedented potency and the fruit.
Because human effort is unitary,
there is only a single instrument;
and because it is pervaded by that cultivation (*bhāvanā*), there is only a single state of being cultivated (*bhāvyatā*).
For this very reason, the Prābhākaras maintain that this is an "expansion of the probandum" (*sādhyavivṛddhi*).
It is the synthesis of the objecthood (*viṣayatva*) and instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).
If that which has become the object is also the instrument, [then there is no contradiction].

Well then, in the case of the injunction "by means of the Darśapūrṇamāsa [sacrifices]," since those factors expressed by the common core (tantra) are connected to the performance through that very same common core, and since the objective domain is one, there would be only a single instrument; consequently, there could be no connection with the procedure (itikartavyatā) in its distinct forms.
It is said: Your Honor, who are learned in the scriptures, has not correctly grasped their words;
for that alone which has become an object is the instrument.
The meaning of "nothing else" is that [the object] exists as an object by virtue of its being a concomitant of cognition.
It is understood according to its designation,
because the designation serves as a means for comprehension;
therefore, by virtue of that designation, the combined [factors] constitute the object.
The instrument (*karaṇa*), however, is that which is invariably connected with the accomplishment of the mandate (*niyoga*);
and it should be understood according to its own nature (*svabhāva*).
For the capacity of means to accomplish their ends depends upon their nature; thus, when there is a difference in nature, there is a difference in their capacity as instruments.

And since it is the instrument (*karaṇa*) by virtue of being the object of the volitional effort (*kṛti*) that brings about accomplishment (*sādhakatva*), its status as an instrument is distinct [from its other roles].

Now, one might ask: if each [element] were thus accepted as an instrument individually, why would they not be the cause for the fulfillment of the mandate (*niyoga*) independently of any other instruments? It is not so;
for the fulfillment of the mandate depends upon the instruments exactly as they are prescribed in the scriptural text.
In that case, since many instruments are heard to produce it, its accomplishment is likewise [achieved] by them;
for it is observed that even a single thing can be produced by multiple instruments.
For example: "He goes by means of a horse, a palanquin, or a chariot" in relation to the act of going.
If it were argued that the causal operation (*vyāpāra*) is distinct in each case,
we certainly accept that even here the intermediate *apūrvas* (unseen potencies) produced by the various acts are distinct as their respective operations.

For this very reason, because the status of being an instrument (*karaṇabhāva*) is differentiated by those [intermediate *apūrvas*], there is no confusion among the ritual properties (*dharma*) of the clarified butter (*ājya*), the vegetable offerings (*auṣadha*), and the milk offerings (*sānnāyya*), even though they are all ultimately prompted by the final *apūrva*.
Because dharmas are situated as the means for accomplishing the *apūrva*,
and because that [accomplishment] is distinct; furthermore, as for those who do not admit an intermediate *bhāvanā* between the sacrifice and the *apūrva*.
The status of those sacrifices and so forth as instruments (*karaṇa*) is difficult to establish;
for the *apūrva* lacks the nature of an activity (*avyāpārarūpatva*), whereas the status of being an instrument arises from a connection with an activity (*vyāpārasambandhaprabhavatva*).
If it is argued that the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is secondary (*gauṇa*),
then how can there be a connection with the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance)?
For it is the instrument that is connected with the *itikartavyatā*.
And that which is secondary (gauṇa) is not an instrument (karaṇa),
for the properties of the primary (mukhya) cannot exist in the secondary.
Even those who assert that the expression of productive activity (bhāvanā) occurs in all verbal suffixes (ākhyāta) [must concede this].
Their view as well does not appeal to us;
for there is no evidence that the *bhāvanā* is denoted by the suffixes *laṭ* and so forth when they do not denote an action (*kārya*).
This concludes the refutation of the Vārtika school’s position.
Furthermore, as for the presentation of the evidence consisting in the observation of the answer, "What does he do? He cooks," that too is not a proving factor.

For this question—"What does he do?"—is specifically about a particular activity (*vyāpāraviśeṣa*). In that context, even by the answer "he cooks" (*pacati*), that very [activity] is indicated. However, it is not merely the utterance of a verbal root (*dhātu*) that expresses activity in general that is being employed.
In that case, since [the utterance] would consist of only that much, it would be a corruption (*apabhraṃśa*);

furthermore, if another suffix were uttered, there would be no connection with the question. For this very reason, forms such as the present indicative are employed when referring to the activity of an insentient entity.
However, the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others are employed only with reference to a conscious agent;
nor is their usage toward insentient things merely figurative, since there is no contradiction in their primary application.
Furthermore, if they were to denote only the number and other attributes of the agent, then in expressions such as “the chariot goes,” they would result in a primary application [of the suffixes].
Nor should it be argued that conjunction and disjunction alone constitute the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*),
while the operation consisting of motion is the meaning of the present tense suffix (*laṭ*) in expressions such as "the chariot goes";
for by this reasoning, the primary meaning of the present tense suffix would apply even to insentient things.
Since it is the verbal roots themselves that express action (*kriyā*), it is logical that the meaning of a root is primarily the operation (*vyāpāra*) itself,
rather than the secondary [results] of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and disjunction (*vibhāga*).
Furthermore, [if it were otherwise], the fault of attributing multiple meanings to a single word would also follow.
Because conjunction by itself cannot be expressed [as "it goes"],
because even when a conjunction is produced by conjunction the term "it goes" is not employed,
and because no usage is observed for a disjunction produced by disjunction;
It is not the case that conjunction or disjunction alone is denoted by the root *gam*;
what is the use of this persistent insistence based on mere intellectual fancy— a childish prattle that only captivates the minds of the ignorant?

This work, which has as its proper subject matter [the exposition of] the Teacher’s doctrine, was composed by Śālikanātha for the sake of accomplishing the benefit of the learned, having thoroughly examined it with correct insight. (2)
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Subject Matter to be Accomplished," in the *Prakaraṇapañcikā* composed by the Great Professor, the venerable Śrīmacchālikanāthamiśra.
